claims.text: Temperature-dependent stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior in HfNbTaTiZr results from coherent nanoprecipitates formed during thermomechanical processing.
The nanoprecipitates have a thermal expansion coefficient different from that of the HfNbTaTiZr matrix.
Thermal expansion mismatch between nanoprecipitates and the matrix generates local residual thermal stresses.
Local residual stresses alter dislocation activation and elastic response over a broad temperature range.
The homogenized initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy has a uniform matrix with minimal pre-existing precipitates.
Aging HfNbTaTiZr at 600–800 °C induces coherent nanoprecipitate formation.
Controlled cooling after aging preserves thermal-expansion-mismatch effects.
Aged samples containing nanoprecipitates will be compared with unaged samples over approximately 293 K to 1250 °C.
Coherent nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces can affect deformation and strengthening behavior.
Residual stress fields from the precipitates modify the energy landscape for dislocation nucleation and mobility.
The proposed residual-stress mechanism affects elastic moduli, high-temperature creep, and work hardening during cold deformation.
Relative to the control, the aged alloy will show anomalous temperature dependence of its elastic moduli, potentially including greater stiffness at intermediate temperatures.
Relative to the control, the aged alloy will show a reduced or otherwise altered creep rate at 1250 °C because local precipitate stress fields impede creep mechanisms.
Relative to the control, the aged alloy will show enhanced hardness after cold rolling because nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces provide additional barriers.
Untreated homogenized HfNbTaTiZr will exhibit more conventional temperature dependence of elastic and creep properties.
The proposed mechanism remains active only while the nanoprecipitates retain suitable nanoscale size and coherency.
If the nanoprecipitates lose coherency or dissolve, the alloy behavior may revert toward the untreated baseline.
Rapid cooling can suppress precipitate formation in the control samples.

Failure to observe significant property differences between aged and control samples, or failure of residual stress to correlate with coherent nanoprecipitates, would refute the proposed governing mechanism.
